subject: B22DAF556BE4E92527A7407F3DDC5630
introduction: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá was often asked in the West whether Bahá’ís believe in reincarnation. His answers, gathered here, are consistent: the individual soul does not come back to this world; what “returns” is a set of qualities, as John the Baptist came “in the spirit and power of Elias” and yet said “I am not” Elias; the soul’s progress is forward through other worlds, “no butterfly goes back into the chrysalis”; and those who believe otherwise should be met at first with tolerance. The Gítá’s worn-out robes and Plato’s soul “born again many times” are the doctrine in its two classic forms, and Wordsworth gives the feeling behind it. The Gospel passages are the ones the readings themselves cite. Hebrews’ “once to die” and Ecclesiastes’ spirit returning to God are the biblical side of the denial, and the question about the man born blind shows the moral use to which the idea is put.
questions: What problem does reincarnation solve for those who believe it? How do the readings propose to solve the same problem?
John “came in the spirit and power of Elias” but said he was not Elias. Explain the distinction the readings draw from this. Is it convincing?
Reading 3 counsels not opposing the belief at first; reading 23 calls it untrue. How should a strongly held disagreement be handled with those who hold the other view?
“No butterfly goes back into the chrysalis.” What does this picture of the soul’s journey assume about this world?

outside.why: “Reincarnation is a very abstruse question.” The doctrine at its most attractive, in the Bhagavad Gítá: as when one layeth his worn-out robes away, and, taking new ones, sayeth, “These will I wear to-day!”, so putteth by the spirit lightly its garb of flesh, and passeth to inherit a residence afresh. What does the image promise, and what do the readings put in its place?

Plato taught it too: the soul, as being immortal, and having been born again many times, has knowledge of all things. The readings deny the return of the individual. What did Plato want the doctrine to explain?
The reading quotes this verse: in my Father’s house are many mansions.
Do not oppose them on this at the beginning; be tolerant. It is good not to do any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth.
In the Gospel, return refers to qualities and not to essence. Of John the Baptist: he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias.
Similar types recur, as the seasons do. One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh; the sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose.
The reading cites this exchange: Art thou Elias? And he saith, I am not.
And this one: if ye will receive it, this is Elias, which was for to come.

Reincarnation as a theory of reward and punishment in this world. The disciples asked of a man born blind: who did sin, this man, or his parents? Jesus refused both explanations. What does the question assume, and what does his answer do to it?
The belief that God gives the soul another chance in another body. It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.
“No one ever returns here.” If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come.
When the soul leaves the body it does not return to the changing world. Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.
“No butterfly goes back into the chrysalis.” When I became a man, I put away childish things.

All who are called into being here are new souls. Wordsworth felt otherwise: the Soul that rises with us, our life’s Star, hath had elsewhere its setting, and cometh from afar. What experiences make people feel they have lived before, and how do the readings account for them?
Those who followed Christ were born of the spirit. Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. How can a man be born when he is old?

One school holds that the spirit is refined through endless births. Rumi’s ascent has no return in it: I died as a plant and rose again an animal; I died as an animal and arose a man. Which do the readings resemble?
Will a soul that has made the circle make it again? The path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.

The belief of “the Hindustani” is described and declined. Vivekananda asked of another faith only this: each must assimilate the spirit of the others and yet preserve his individuality. How do readings 3 and 23 differ in tone toward those who hold the doctrine?

shortfall: Readings 4, 7, 8, 10 to 12, 17, 20, 23 and 24 restate the denial, or the distinction between return of qualities and return of persons, in other words.
